e.etymology: The Turkish form of Arabic Isra, 'night journey', the name of the Prophet Muhammad's journey from Mecca to Jerusalem. Esra is also the German and Scandinavian spelling of the Biblical Ezra.
A Latin American spelling of Johan or Joan, forms of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. The Jh- spelling is most common in Colombia, Venezuela and the Dominican Republic.
A recent American name of unclear source. Baby-name sites call it Native American for 'warrior of life', but no source language has been identified.
A spelling of Trey, the word for a three in cards and dice, from Old French treis. It began as a nickname for a boy who is the third of his name.

e.meaning: Miguel (who is like God?) joined with Angel (angel)
e.etymology: The Spanish double name Miguel Angel written as one word. Miguel is Michael, Hebrew for 'who is like God?', and Angel is 'angel'; the pair honors the archangel Michael and matches Italian Michelangelo.
A modern American name that sets Gray on the -den ending of Brayden and Hayden. It also serves as a spelling of the English surname Graydon.
From Arabic salim, 'safe' or 'sound', from the root s-l-m that also gives salaam, 'peace', and Islam.
From the revolutionary pseudonym of Vladimir Lenin, thought to come from the Siberian river Lena. It has been used as a first name in Latin America and India since the 20th century.

assoc.t: Vladimir Lenin, founder of the Soviet Union
sounds like Lennon, as in John Lennon of the Beatles

e.note: Most Americans will think first of the Soviet revolutionary leader.

e.etymology: A German pet form of Margarete (Margaret), from Greek margarites, 'pearl'. It is known everywhere from the Brothers Grimm tale Hansel and Gretel.
namesakes: Gretel (sister in the Grimm fairy tale Hansel and Gretel)

assoc.t: Gretel of the fairy tale Hansel and Gretel

e.etymology: A spelling of Aliyah or Aaliyah, from Arabic Aliya, 'exalted' or 'sublime', the feminine of Ali. It also matches Hebrew aliyah, 'ascent'.

assoc.t: sounds like Aaliyah, the late R&B singer

e.etymology: A respelling of Riley, which comes both from an English place name, Old English for 'rye clearing', and from the Irish surname Reilly, 'descendant of Raghallach'.
From Arabic qasim, 'one who divides or distributes', from the verb qasama. Qasim was the first son of the Prophet Muhammad, who is called Abu al-Qasim after him.
The German form of Odilia, a feminine name built on the Germanic root od, 'wealth' or 'fortune', the same root as Otto. Saint Odile is the patron of Alsace.
The Hebrew form of Benjamin, from ben, 'son', and yamin, 'right hand' or 'south'. In Genesis he is the youngest son of Jacob and Rachel and the ancestor of one of the twelve tribes.
namesakes: Binyamin Netanyahu (Israeli prime minister, Benjamin in English)

e.etymology: A recent American name close in sound to Alaya, Elia and Eliana. No single source is established.
A recent American coinage in the pattern of Jamir, Kymir and Zymir, names that put a new first syllable on Amir, Arabic for 'prince' or 'commander'.
The East Slavic form of Helga, from Old Norse heilagr, 'holy'. Saint Olga of Kiev, a 10th-century ruler, made it a classic in Russia and Ukraine; English borrowed it in the 19th century.
From Greek Eugenia, the feminine of Eugenios (Eugene), from eu, 'well', and genes, 'born'. Saint Eugenia of Rome was an early Christian martyr.

assoc.t: Eugenia, a genus of evergreen shrubs used for hedges

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Herbert, from the Germanic elements hari, 'army', and berht, 'bright'.
An anglicized form of Irish Una, possibly from uan, 'lamb'. Edmund Spenser used Una in The Faerie Queene with the Latin sense 'one', and in the Balkans the name recalls the river Una.
e.note: In Spanish and Italian, una is the feminine word for 'a' or 'one'.

e.etymology: A pet form of Virginia, and sometimes of Ginevra or Genevieve. Virginia comes from the Roman family name Verginius, later linked with Latin virgo, 'maiden'.
namesakes: Ginny Weasley (Ron's sister in the Harry Potter series)
Ginny Miller (teen lead of the Netflix series Ginny & Georgia)

assoc.t: Ginny Weasley of the Harry Potter series

e.etymology: A German pet form of Friedrich (Frederick), from the Germanic elements frid, 'peace', and ric, 'ruler'. Frederick the Great of Prussia was nicknamed Old Fritz.
namesakes: Fritz the Cat (R. Crumb's comic-strip cat)

assoc.t: on the fritz, meaning broken or out of order
Fritz, wartime slang for a German soldier
Fritz the Cat, R. Crumb's comic-strip cat

e.note: On the fritz means broken, and Fritz was wartime slang for a German soldier.

e.etymology: From Sanskrit nikhila, 'whole, entire, complete'. It is a common men's name across India and Nepal.
A spelling of Arlene (also Arline), a name of unknown source that drew notice as the heroine of Balfe's 1843 opera The Bohemian Girl. For boys it follows Arlen.
From Irish cael (modern caol), 'slender', the name of a warrior of the Fianna in Irish legend. The same Gaelic word, in the sense 'narrows' or 'strait', lies behind Kyle.
e.note: Sounds the same as kale, the leafy green.

e.etymology: A respelling of Mason, an English occupational surname for a stoneworker, from Old French masson.

assoc.t: Edward Masen, Edward Cullen's human name in Twilight

e.etymology: A spelling of Maddox, a Welsh surname meaning 'son of Madoc'. Madoc (Madog) is an old Welsh name from mad, 'fortunate' or 'good'.
The feminine of Latin divinus, 'divine, of a god', and the everyday word for divine in Spanish, Italian and Portuguese. It is a traditional given name in the Philippines.
A modern Indian girls' name that Indian name lists gloss as 'heaven'; it is close to Sanskrit words for the sky such as vihayas.
A recent American coinage that reads as Avery with an added M, echoing Maverick and Mavis.
Created for Jinora, the young airbending master and granddaughter of Aang in the animated series The Legend of Korra (2012 to 2014).
namesakes: Jinora (airbender in The Legend of Korra)

assoc.t: Jinora, airbender in The Legend of Korra

e.etymology: From Greek Rhode, from rhodon, 'rose', or 'woman from Rhodes'. In Acts 12 Rhoda is the servant girl who hears Peter knocking at the door; English Protestants took up the name in the 17th century.
namesakes: Rhoda Morgenstern (title character of the 1970s sitcom Rhoda)

assoc.t: Rhoda Morgenstern of the 1970s sitcom Rhoda
